title: Shocking study proves chocolate for breakfast turns children into maths stars
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the full paper, with no sign-up.
overview: The study asks whether chocolate at breakfast raises children's maths scores. It treats sugar as instant fuel for the brain. It does not mention earlier research on the 'sugar crash' (tiredness after a burst of sugar).
methods: On three mornings, N=12 children in one classroom ate chocolate for breakfast and then took a maths test. There was no control group eating an ordinary breakfast. Data availability: The test scores are not shared, for 'commercial' reasons linked to the chocolate brand, the authors say.
conclusion: The authors conclude that chocolate breakfasts make children better at maths. They call for chocolate at every school breakfast to raise national exam results.
source: The journal charged the authors £1,800 and published the paper five days after it arrived. Its website names no editors and says nothing about peer review.

feedback.summary: Five of the six criteria are weak. The journal took a fee, published within five days and names no editors. Twelve children ate chocolate with no control group, the scores are hidden and the authors still call for chocolate at every school breakfast. Free access cannot make up for this, so it sits at the bottom of the scale.

title.note: 'Shocking', 'proves' and 'maths stars' are press-release hype and promise far more than a test of 12 children on three mornings could show.

access.note: Anyone can read the full paper free online with no sign-up; Access is about how open a paper is, not whether the study is any good.

source.note: A £1,800 fee, publication five days after the paper arrived, no named editors and no word on peer review point to a predatory journal.

theory.note: It treats sugar as instant fuel for the brain and ignores earlier research on the 'sugar crash', so it does not build on what is already known.

methods.note: Only 12 children in one class were tested on three mornings, with no control group on an ordinary breakfast and no shared scores.

conclusion.note: Without a comparison group the test cannot show that chocolate caused anything, yet the authors claim it does and want it at every school breakfast.

title: New titanium alloy will make aircraft lighter
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can download the full paper as a PDF.
overview: Earlier studies found that light titanium-aluminium alloys (mixtures of metals) lose strength when they get hot. This study looks for a mix that does not, building on existing models of how metal behaves under stress.
methods: The team heated and pulled N=500 new alloy bars until they cracked, comparing them with a current aircraft alloy. Data availability: Test logs and code are free online. The exact recipe is withheld until a patent (a legal right to an invention) is granted.
conclusion: The authors report that the alloy kept its strength when hot and would make parts about 15% lighter. They add that it has only been tested in the lab and is currently too expensive for commercial use.
source: It appeared in a materials science journal run by a large engineering society. Two outside experts checked it before publication (peer review).

feedback.summary: Free access, peer review in a society journal and a clear gap to fill are strong points. The team tested 500 bars against a current alloy, shared their logs and code and stated their limits openly. It falls just short of the top because the title says the alloy 'will' make aircraft lighter and the recipe is withheld.

title.note: It names the finding, but 'will make aircraft lighter' sounds certain and leaves out that the alloy is only lab-tested and too expensive to use yet.

access.note: Anyone can download the full paper free as a PDF, so every reader can check the claims for themselves.

source.note: It appeared in a journal run by a large engineering society and two outside experts checked it before publication (peer review).

theory.note: It starts from the known problem of light titanium-aluminium alloys losing strength when hot and builds on existing models of how metal behaves under stress.

methods.note: Testing 500 bars against a current aircraft alloy, with logs and code free online, is thorough, though the withheld recipe stops others fully repeating it.

conclusion.note: The authors report the strength and weight results but add that the alloy has only been tested in the lab and is too expensive for now.

title: Late-night phone use makes adults take longer to fall asleep
access: Not free to everyone: readers need a university login or must email the authors for a copy.
overview: Lab studies show that blue light from screens lowers melatonin (a hormone that makes us sleepy). Few have checked whether this matters outside the lab. This one asks whether adults who use phones late at night take longer to fall asleep.
methods: The researchers surveyed N=2,000 adults once, without sleep trackers. People estimated their late-night phone use and how long they took to fall asleep. Data availability: Only summary tables are shared, not the raw answers, to protect privacy.
conclusion: The authors report that late phone use goes with taking longer to fall asleep. They say this does not show that phones cause the delay. It may run the other way: people who cannot sleep may reach for their phones.
source: It appeared in a peer-reviewed general science journal published by a national academy of sciences.

feedback.summary: Its strengths are a peer-reviewed academy journal, a clear gap to fill outside the lab and a conclusion that does not claim cause. It is held back by a one-off survey of people's own estimates, no shared raw answers and the need for a login or a request. The title also says phone use 'makes' adults slower to fall asleep.

title.note: It reports the finding plainly, but 'makes' states a cause that a one-off survey cannot show and that the authors themselves avoid claiming.

access.note: Only some people can read it, because you need a university login or must email the authors for a copy.

source.note: It was peer reviewed and appeared in a general science journal published by a national academy of sciences.

theory.note: It builds on lab evidence that blue light lowers melatonin and fills a clear gap by asking whether this matters outside the lab.

methods.note: The sample of 2,000 adults is large, but each person was surveyed once and estimated their own phone use and sleep, with only summary tables shared.

conclusion.note: The authors speak only of a link and say it may run the other way, since people who cannot sleep may reach for their phones.

title: A daily cup of herbal tea may help keep the mind sharp
access: Free to everyone online. As at many free journals, the authors paid a fee so readers do not have to.
overview: Drawing on folk medicine, the study asks whether daily herbal tea protects against Alzheimer's disease. It does not mention amyloid plaques or tau tangles, protein build-ups in the brain that mark the disease.
methods: For six weeks, the researchers followed N=40 adults who already drank the tea daily, with no comparison group. Memory was checked in short phone calls, not the in-person tests doctors use. Data availability: Raw data are not shared, to protect participants' privacy.
conclusion: The authors conclude that the tea protects brain cells and helps prevent Alzheimer's disease. Their main evidence is that participants said they felt more alert after six weeks.
source: The journal's website has many spelling mistakes and promises 'publication within 48 hours for a fee'. It does not say whether outside experts check papers.

feedback.summary: The journal sells publication within 48 hours and says nothing about peer review. Forty people who already drank the tea were followed with no comparison group. Yet the authors claim the tea helps prevent Alzheimer's because people felt more alert. A calm title and free access cannot rescue it, so it sits at the bottom of the scale.

title.note: 'May help' sounds careful, but the title leaves out that only 40 people who already drank the tea were followed for six weeks.

access.note: Anyone can read it free online, so it is fully open, even though free access says nothing about whether the findings are right.

source.note: A website with many spelling mistakes, a promise of 'publication within 48 hours for a fee' and no word on outside checks mark a predatory journal.

theory.note: It draws on folk medicine and ignores amyloid plaques and tau tangles, the brain changes that mark Alzheimer's, so it does not build on earlier science.

methods.note: Only 40 people who already drank the tea were followed, with no comparison group, short phone calls instead of the tests doctors use and no shared data.

conclusion.note: Claiming the tea protects brain cells and helps prevent Alzheimer's is a huge leap from people saying they felt more alert after six weeks.

title: Field trial finds no clear effect of one pesticide on bees' ability to fly home, at current farm doses
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can download the full paper.
overview: Lab studies found that this pesticide made bees lose their way. This study asks whether that happens on real farms at the doses farmers use.
methods: Over two years, N=6,000 bees on 20 farms wore small radio tags recording whether they flew home. Half the farms, picked at random, used the pesticide, following a preregistered plan. Data availability: All data and code are free online.
conclusion: The authors report no clear harm to bees' ability to fly home at current farm doses. They say a small effect is possible and warn against applying the result to other insects.
source: It appeared in a peer-reviewed ecology journal run by a large scientific society. The pesticide's maker paid for half the trial and saw the results before publication. The authors declare this conflict of interest.

feedback.summary: Free access, an exact title, a randomised and preregistered field trial with open data and a careful conclusion stand out. It is held back because the pesticide's maker paid for half the trial and saw the results before publication, so readers cannot rule out that this shaped what was reported, even though the authors declared it.

title.note: It names the design, the single pesticide, the finding and its key limit, 'at current farm doses', without overstating anything.

access.note: Anyone can download the full paper free online, so every reader can check the methods for themselves.

source.note: The society journal uses peer review, but the pesticide's maker paid for half the trial and saw the results first, a declared conflict of interest.

theory.note: It fills a clear gap by testing whether the lab finding that the pesticide made bees lose their way holds up on real farms.

methods.note: The farms using the pesticide were picked at random, the plan was preregistered, 6,000 bees were tracked over two years and all data and code are free online.

conclusion.note: The authors claim only what they tested, admit a small effect is possible and warn against applying the result to other insects.

title: Instagram use raises anxiety in teenagers, survey finds
access: Not free to everyone: the full paper needs a university library login.
overview: The study uses the idea of social comparison: people can feel worse after comparing themselves with others. It assumes Instagram use leads directly to anxiety and does not discuss other causes of teenage anxiety.
methods: The researchers surveyed N=5,000 teenagers once (a cross-sectional study). Teenagers reported their own hours on Instagram and their own anxiety. Data availability: Summary figures are in the paper; raw data are available from the lead author on request.
conclusion: The authors report that teenagers who used Instagram more reported more anxiety. They mostly call this a link but hint in places that Instagram is the cause. They do not ask whether anxious teenagers simply use social media more.
source: It appeared in a peer-reviewed psychology journal. The journal's website says it wants 'findings that get people talking'. It sends press releases to journalists for most papers.

feedback.summary: A large survey in a peer-reviewed journal gives a fair base. But teenagers reported their own Instagram use and anxiety only once, which can show a link but not a cause. The title and authors lean towards cause, the journal seeks attention and the paper needs a login. Every criterion lands in the middle, so the study does too.

title.note: 'Survey finds' is honest about the design, but 'raises anxiety' claims a cause that a one-off survey cannot show.

access.note: Only some people can read it, because the full paper needs a university library login.

source.note: It is peer reviewed, but the journal says it wants 'findings that get people talking' and sends press releases about most papers.

theory.note: It uses the known idea of social comparison but assumes Instagram leads straight to anxiety and ignores other causes of teenage anxiety.

methods.note: Surveying 5,000 teenagers gives a large sample, but each was asked only once about their own hours and anxiety, with raw data only on request.

conclusion.note: Calling the result a link fits the data, but the authors hint at cause and never ask whether anxious teenagers simply use social media more.

title: Revolutionary AI hiring tool ends gender bias for good
access: Free to download, but only for people who give the company a work email address.
overview: The company assumes that hiding names from the software removes gender bias. It does not mention proxy variables. These are CV details, such as a women's college or sports team, that hint at gender.
methods: The tool was trained and tested on N=2,400 old CVs from years when 80% of hires were men. The report does not compare how men and women were scored. Data availability: The company does not share the data or code, which it calls its own property.
conclusion: The company concludes that its tool removes gender bias from hiring because it never sees names. It recommends the tool to all employers.
source: This is a white paper (a report a company publishes itself) about a product the same company sells. No outside experts checked it.

feedback.summary: A company's own report, checked by no outside experts, claims its product ends gender bias. The tool learned from old CVs, from years when 80% of hires were men. The report never compares how men and women were scored and shares no data. With five of six criteria weak, it sits at the bottom of the scale.

title.note: 'Revolutionary' and 'ends gender bias for good' are sales hype promising total success that the report never actually measured.

access.note: Only some people can read it, because the company asks for a work email address before you can download it.

source.note: It is a white paper the company published about its own product with no outside experts checking it, so it works as marketing.

theory.note: It assumes hiding names removes gender bias and ignores proxy variables, CV details such as a women's college that still hint at gender.

methods.note: The tool learned from 2,400 CVs from years when most hires were men, the report never compares scores by gender and no data or code are shared.

conclusion.note: Claiming bias is gone because the tool never sees names, then recommending it to all employers, rests on a guess the report never tested.

title: New layer raises perovskite solar cell efficiency from 22.0% to 23.5%, but cells break down faster in damp air
access: Not free to everyone: the full paper needs a university login, but the authors email copies on request.
overview: Perovskite solar cells (a newer, cheaper type) are known to lose power in the layer that carries charge. Using research on why their crystals break down, the study tests a new layer.
methods: The team tested N=240 cells, half with the new layer, under artificial sunlight and in damp air. A second, independent lab repeated the tests. Data availability: All results are published, but the exact recipe is withheld until a patent is granted.
conclusion: The authors call the gain in efficiency (sunlight turned into power) small. They say the cells are not ready to sell because they break down faster in damp air.
source: It appeared in a peer-reviewed journal covering all of science that accepts under one in ten papers.

feedback.summary: A selective peer-reviewed journal, an exact title and a test of 240 cells repeated by an independent lab make this strong. The authors also admit the cells break down faster in damp air. It falls just short of the top because readers need a login or a request and the recipe is withheld for a patent.

title.note: It gives the exact gain from 22.0% to 23.5% and the key limit that the cells break down faster in damp air.

access.note: Only some people can read it, because the full paper needs a university login, though the authors email copies on request.

source.note: It appeared in a very selective peer-reviewed journal covering all of science, which accepts under one in ten papers.

theory.note: It targets the known problem of power loss in the layer that carries charge and builds on research into why perovskite crystals break down.

methods.note: Comparing 240 cells with and without the new layer, with an independent lab repeating the tests, is thorough, though the withheld recipe means others cannot make the same cells.

conclusion.note: The authors call the gain in efficiency small and say the cells are not ready to sell because they break down faster in damp air.

title: Shocking brain scans prove violent video games numb young people to real pain
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £35. No free copy is available.
overview: Earlier research suggests that repeatedly seeing violence can make people react less to it (desensitisation). This study asks whether that shows up in brain blood flow. The authors do not explain how blood flow links to feelings or actions.
methods: The team randomly gave N=60 university students a violent game or a puzzle game for 20 minutes. A scanner then recorded their brain blood flow as they viewed injury photos; the analysis plan was not registered in advance. Data availability: The data are not shared.
conclusion: After the violent game, students' brains reacted less to the photos. The authors conclude that violent games numb young people to real suffering and help cause violence in society.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed psychology journal. Other scientists have criticised it in print for accepting small brain-scan studies with big claims.

feedback.summary: Randomly giving students a violent or puzzle game is a fair test in a peer-reviewed journal, which keeps it off the bottom. But the analysis plan was not registered, the data are not shared and the paper is paywalled. The title and conclusion leap from one lab measure of brain blood flow to claims about real pain and violence.

title.note: 'Shocking' and 'prove' are hype words, and the title turns a lab measure of brain blood flow in 60 students into proof that games numb young people to real pain.

access.note: At £35 with no free copy, almost no one can read the full paper without paying, so few readers can check the claims for themselves.

source.note: It is peer reviewed, but other scientists have criticised the journal in print for accepting small brain-scan studies with big claims, so its approval counts for less.

theory.note: It builds on earlier research on desensitisation (reacting less to violence after seeing a lot of it), but never explains how brain blood flow links to feelings or actions.

methods.note: Randomly giving 60 students a violent or a puzzle game is a fair comparison, but the analysis plan was not registered in advance and the data are not shared.

conclusion.note: One brain measure taken after a 20-minute game cannot show that games numb young people to real suffering, let alone that they help cause violence in society.

title: Plastic found in our blood is making us ill, scientists warn
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read and download the full paper.
overview: Earlier studies found tiny pieces of plastic in food, water and air, but no test could detect them in human blood. This study asks whether such plastic gets into our blood.
methods: The team built a new, very sensitive chemical test and used it on blood from N=400 healthy adult donors. To catch plastic from lab equipment, they ran samples of pure water through every step. Data availability: The full method and the results for every sample, without donors' names, are free to download.
conclusion: Plastic was found in 308 of the 400 samples. The authors say the health effects of these amounts are unknown and call for urgent research.
source: Published in a large general science journal that turns down nine in ten papers. Independent experts and a statistics specialist reviewed it. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

feedback.summary: Free access, a selective journal with expert and statistics review, a clear gap in knowledge, 400 donors, checks for plastic from lab equipment, open data and a cautious conclusion put this near the top. Only the title lets it down: it says the plastic is making us ill, which the authors say is still unknown.

title.note: Saying the plastic 'is making us ill' claims a harm the study never measured, and 'scientists warn' credits it to authors who say the health effects are unknown.

access.note: Anyone can read and download the full paper free online, so everyone can check the method and results for themselves.

source.note: A general science journal that turns down nine in ten papers had independent experts and a statistics specialist check the study, and the authors declare no conflicts.

theory.note: It fills a clear gap: earlier studies found plastic in food, water and air, but no test could detect it in human blood.

methods.note: A new, very sensitive test on 400 donors, pure-water checks for plastic from lab equipment and free results for every sample make this careful, open work.

conclusion.note: It reports what was found (plastic in 308 of 400 samples) and says plainly that the health effects of these amounts are unknown.

title: Male bosses of the 500 largest US companies are taller than the average US man
access: Free to everyone online as a preprint (an early paper shared before review).
overview: The authors argue that early hunter-gatherers chose tall men as leaders. They say the same instinct still picks company bosses but give no evidence. The paper does not mention the 'halo effect' (when one liked trait, such as height, colours how we judge someone).
methods: The authors collected the heights of N=452 men who led the 500 largest US companies. They compared these with the national average but did not measure profits or leadership skill. Data availability: A spreadsheet of heights is available from the authors on request.
conclusion: The bosses were about 6 cm taller than average. The authors conclude that tall men are born to lead and that evolution explains why companies choose them.
source: Posted on a public preprint server. It has not been peer reviewed or accepted by a journal.

feedback.summary: An exact title and free access are real strengths. But the paper has not been peer reviewed, it offers no evidence for its evolutionary story about the height gap, it ignores the halo effect (height colouring how we judge people) and it claims tall men are born to lead. These faults weigh far more than its strengths.

title.note: It states only what was measured, that male bosses of the 500 largest US companies are taller than the average US man, with no claim about why.

access.note: Anyone can read the preprint free online, though being free to read says nothing about whether its claims are correct.

source.note: It is a preprint on a public server, so no independent experts have checked it (peer review) and no journal has accepted it yet.

theory.note: It says a hunter-gatherer instinct picks bosses but gives no evidence and ignores the halo effect (one liked trait, such as height, colouring how we judge someone).

methods.note: Comparing the heights of 452 bosses with the national average can show a gap, but nothing measured leadership skill or profits and the data are only on request.

conclusion.note: Claiming that tall men are born to lead because of evolution treats a height gap as proof of inborn ability, when people may simply tend to pick tall men.

title: Miracle lavender oil beats sleeping pills for insomnia
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £32. No free copy is available.
overview: A few studies suggest lavender scent calms the brain by acting on GABA (a chemical messenger that helps us relax). How this works is unclear. This trial asks whether lavender helps people with mild insomnia (trouble sleeping) fall asleep sooner.
methods: The trial randomly split N=60 adults into three groups for two weeks: lavender on the pillow, a placebo scent or nothing. People knew whether they had lavender and rated their own sleep in diaries; no one took sleeping pills. Data availability: Only summary figures are shared.
conclusion: People using lavender said they fell asleep 15 minutes sooner on average than the placebo group. The authors conclude that lavender oil is a natural alternative to sleeping pills.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed journal on natural remedies. Most trials it publishes have fewer than 60 people and are rarely cited by other researchers.

feedback.summary: Splitting 60 adults into groups at random, with a placebo scent for comparison, is a fair start that keeps this trial off the bottom. But people knew whether they had lavender and rated their own sleep, the paper is paywalled and the title and conclusion compare lavender with sleeping pills, which no one in the trial took.

title.note: 'Miracle' is a hype word, and 'beats sleeping pills' describes a contest that never happened, since no one in the trial took sleeping pills.

access.note: At £32 with no free copy, almost no one can read the full paper without paying, so few readers can check how the trial was run.

source.note: It is peer reviewed, but most trials in this natural remedies journal have fewer than 60 people and are rarely cited, so its approval reassures less.

theory.note: It builds on a few studies suggesting lavender acts on GABA (a chemical messenger that helps us relax), but how this would work is still unclear.

methods.note: Randomly splitting 60 adults into lavender, placebo and no-scent groups helps, but people knew if they had lavender, rated their own sleep and only summary figures are shared.

conclusion.note: Calling lavender an alternative to sleeping pills goes far beyond a self-reported 15-minute gain over a placebo scent in a trial with no sleeping pill group.

title: Stomachs of 300 foxes from three cities show a diet high in human food waste
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £38. No free copy is available.
overview: Many studies show that animals that eat almost anything, such as foxes, switch easily to nearby food. This study applies that well-known idea to city foxes and human food waste.
methods: The team examined the stomachs of N=300 foxes killed on roads in three cities over five years. They compared these with 120 rural foxes. Data availability: Summary tables are in the paper; full data are on request, but two teams waited over six months.
conclusion: The authors conclude that city foxes rely heavily on human food waste, which may affect their health and numbers. They note that stomach contents show only the last few meals.
source: Published in the peer-reviewed journal of a large national zoology society. At least two independent experts check each paper.

feedback.summary: A peer-reviewed society journal, 300 foxes over five years, a rural comparison and an exact title are clear strengths. But the paper is paywalled, two teams waited over six months for the full data and it applies a familiar idea. The conclusion's point that the diet may affect the foxes' health and numbers goes beyond what stomach contents show.

title.note: It names the method, the sample, the three cities and the finding in plain words, with no hype and no claim about health.

access.note: At £38 with no free copy, almost no one can read the full paper without paying, although Access is about openness, not whether the findings are correct.

source.note: It appears in the peer-reviewed journal of a large national zoology society, where at least two independent experts check every paper.

theory.note: It rests on many studies showing that animals that eat almost anything switch easily to nearby food, but applies this well-known idea rather than building a new argument.

methods.note: Examining 300 road-killed foxes over five years, with 120 rural foxes for comparison, is a good design, but two teams waited over six months for the full data.

conclusion.note: It notes that stomachs show only the last few meals, but saying the diet may affect the foxes' health and numbers goes beyond what the study measured.

title: Breakthrough: scientists grow a Martian harvest ready to feed future astronauts
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read and download the full paper.
overview: Future crews on Mars will need to grow food in local soil. Earlier work showed that plants can sprout in imitation Mars soil, but not whether the crops are safe to eat.
methods: In a greenhouse, the team grew N=480 plants of ten crops with four fertilisers. Half grew in imitation Mars soil and half in ordinary Earth soil, which formed the control group. Data availability: All plant growth, soil and watering records are free to download.
conclusion: Most crops grew, but they took up heavy metals (toxic metals such as lead) from the imitation soil. The authors warn that the crops would be unsafe to eat without further treatment.
source: Published in the peer-reviewed journal of an international society of planetary scientists. A public science agency funded the work; the authors declare no conflicts of interest.

feedback.summary: Free access, a peer-reviewed society journal, public funding, a clear gap, an Earth-soil control group, open records and an honest warning that the crops would be unsafe to eat untreated make this a very strong study. Only the title holds it back: 'Breakthrough' is hype and 'ready to feed' says the opposite of what the authors found.

title.note: 'Breakthrough' is a hype word, and 'ready to feed future astronauts' hides that the crops took up heavy metals from imitation soil and would be unsafe to eat untreated.

access.note: Anyone can read and download the full paper free online, so pupils, teachers and scientists can all check the work.

source.note: It appears in the peer-reviewed journal of an international society of planetary scientists, with public funding and no declared conflicts of interest.

theory.note: It fills a clear gap: earlier work showed plants can sprout in imitation Mars soil, but not whether the crops would be safe to eat.

methods.note: Growing 480 plants of ten crops, half in Earth soil as a control group, and sharing every growth, soil and watering record makes this careful, open work.

conclusion.note: It reports that most crops grew but warns plainly that they took up heavy metals and would be unsafe to eat without further treatment.

title: Ten minutes of Mozart sharpens students' thinking
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £34. No free copy is available.
overview: The study revives the 'Mozart effect', the idea that Mozart's music makes people cleverer. Later reviews of many studies found little or no effect. The paper does not mention these reviews or the simpler idea that music briefly lifts mood.
methods: Each of N=30 students did a short logic puzzle straight after 10 minutes of Mozart and another after silence. Half heard the music first, to cancel out gains from practice; the prediction was not registered in advance. Data availability: Each student's scores are in the journal's online data archive.
conclusion: Scores were 2 points out of 40 higher after the music. The authors conclude that classical music raises IQ (general intelligence) and advise students to listen before exams.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed psychology journal with a low impact factor. It often prints short studies with surprising results that attract press coverage.

feedback.summary: A sensible test in which half the students heard the music first, with every score shared, is the main strength. But the study revives the Mozart effect without mentioning reviews that found little or no effect, is paywalled and turns a 2-point gain on one puzzle into a claim that music raises IQ. These faults outweigh that strength.

title.note: It avoids hype words, but saying Mozart 'sharpens' thinking sounds broader and more lasting than a 2-point gain on one puzzle straight after the music.

access.note: At £34 with no free copy, almost no one can read the full paper without paying, which makes the IQ claim hard for the public to check.

source.note: It is peer reviewed, but the journal has a low impact factor (its papers are cited less than most) and often prints short, surprising studies that attract press coverage.

theory.note: It revives the Mozart effect without mentioning reviews that found little or no effect and ignores the simpler idea that music briefly lifts mood.

methods.note: Testing 30 students after both music and silence, half hearing the music first, is sensible and every score is shared, but 30 is small and the prediction was not registered.

conclusion.note: A 2-point gain on one puzzle straight after the music cannot show that classical music raises IQ, which was never measured, so the exam advice goes too far.

title: Five electric car models lost 20% to 35% of their range at −10°C in test chambers
access: Free to everyone online: the full report is on the institute's website.
overview: Cold thickens the liquid inside lithium-ion batteries, so they deliver power less easily. Earlier tests have measured this many times. The report asks how much range five current models lose in the cold.
methods: The team tested one car each of N=5 popular models in temperature-controlled chambers at +20°C and −10°C. Each car drove the same set routine three times at each temperature. Data availability: Test plans and battery readings for every car are on the same website.
conclusion: Range fell by 20% to 35%, depending on the model. The authors say this confirms a known limit of current batteries. They advise drivers in cold places to allow for shorter range.
source: Published by a government-funded transport research institute that takes no money from car makers. Two outside battery experts reviewed the report.

feedback.summary: An independent institute, outside expert review, free access, controlled chamber tests, shared readings and a careful conclusion are clear strengths. Two things hold it back. It measures an effect that earlier tests have shown many times, rather than filling a new gap. It also tested only one car of each of five models.

title.note: It gives the number of models, the size of the range loss, the temperature and the test chambers, so it says exactly what was found and how.

access.note: Anyone can read the full report free on the institute's website, along with the test plans and battery readings.

source.note: The report comes from a government-funded institute that takes no money from car makers, and two outside battery experts reviewed it.

theory.note: The battery science is sound and well known, but earlier tests have measured this many times, so new figures for five current models fill no clear gap.

methods.note: Chamber tests with the same routine run three times at each temperature are tightly controlled and fully shared, but one car of each of five models is a small sample.

conclusion.note: It reports a 20% to 35% range loss, calls it a known limit of current batteries and gives practical advice without claiming more than the tests show.

title: In an online survey, 68% of 2,000 workers said they felt more productive at home
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can download the full report as a PDF.
overview: The report asks whether staff get more done working from home than in an office. It mentions no earlier research on productivity or on how people behave at work.
methods: The firm surveyed N=2,000 workers online, measuring productivity with one question: 'Do you feel more productive at home?' Nobody recorded actual output, such as tasks finished. Data availability: The firm keeps the answers private.
conclusion: Because 68% answered 'yes', the report concludes that working from home makes staff more productive. It advises employers to switch to remote working, using software such as the firm's own.
source: A consultancy firm (a company that advises businesses) that sells remote-working software wrote and published the report. No outside experts checked it.

feedback.summary: A firm that sells remote-working software ran this survey. It asked one question about how productive people felt, recorded no real output, kept the answers private and mentioned no earlier research. Yet it says home working makes staff more productive. An honest title and a free download lift it just off the bottom of the scale.

title.note: It names the online survey and the 2,000 workers and says they felt more productive, so readers can tell the result rests on what people said, not measured output.

access.note: Anyone can download the full report free online, though Access is about how open a report is, not whether its findings are right.

source.note: A firm that sells remote-working software wrote and published the report itself with no outside checks, so it has a conflict of interest.

theory.note: The report mentions no earlier research on productivity or on how people behave at work, so it does not build on anything already known.

methods.note: A sample of 2,000 cannot make up for one question about feelings, no record of real output such as tasks finished and answers kept private.

conclusion.note: It treats 68% saying they felt more productive as proof that home working makes staff more productive, then advises employers to use software such as the firm's own.

title: Breakthrough study shows gut bacteria are the main cause of depression
access: Not free to everyone: readers need a university library login.
overview: Research on the gut-brain axis (links between gut and brain) suggests gut bacteria can affect mood. Treating depression as mainly a gut problem, the authors ask whether bacteria from people with depression change how mice behave.
methods: The team gave N=40 germ-free mice (raised with no microbes) gut bacteria from 10 adults with depression or 10 without. Rules for scoring the mice's behaviour were preregistered. Data availability: The data are available from the authors on request.
conclusion: Mice given bacteria from people with depression gave up sooner in stress tests. The authors say gut bacteria may play a part in human depression too. They do not discuss other causes, such as trauma.
source: Published in an often-cited, peer-reviewed journal about bacteria and other microbes (tiny living things), run by a large scientific society. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

feedback.summary: A mouse experiment with preregistered scoring rules in an often-cited society journal has real strengths. But the title calls gut bacteria the main cause of depression, which a mouse study cannot show. Treating depression as mainly a gut problem, data only on request and a library login also hold it back. It sits in the middle of the scale.

title.note: 'Breakthrough' is a hype word and 'the main cause of depression' goes far beyond an experiment in 40 mice, which the title never mentions.

access.note: Only people with a university library login can read the full paper, so many readers cannot check the work for themselves.

source.note: It appeared in an often-cited, peer-reviewed journal about microbes run by a large scientific society, with no conflicts of interest declared.

theory.note: It builds on real research into the gut-brain axis (links between gut and brain), but treating depression as mainly a gut problem leaves out its other causes.

methods.note: Mice given bacteria from people with or without depression were compared using preregistered scoring rules, but each group had only 10 donors and data are available only on request.

conclusion.note: The authors say gut bacteria 'may play a part' in human depression, which fits the mouse results, but they do not discuss other causes such as trauma.

title: Tree rings suggest recent Northern Hemisphere summers are the warmest in 2,000 years
access: Not free to everyone: the journal version needs a university login. A copy from the authors turns up only by searching university online archives.
overview: Tree rings grow wider in warm summers, so they record past temperatures. Earlier records covered only a few centuries or regions. Using methods from earlier studies that match ring widths to thermometer readings, this study looks back 2,000 years.
methods: The team combined N=2,860 tree-ring records from forests across Europe and Asia. Statistical models allowed for gaps, unusual values and uncertainty. Data availability: All records and code are free in a public climate data archive.
conclusion: The authors report that recent summers were the warmest in 2,000 years. They give margins of error and say the result covers only Northern Hemisphere summers in the regions studied.
source: Published in one of the most widely cited science journals. Three climate scientists and a statistics expert reviewed it.

feedback.summary: Experts in climate and statistics reviewed this study for a widely cited journal. It combines 2,860 tree-ring records, shares all records and code and gives margins of error and clear limits. The university login and hard-to-find copy from the authors affect who can read it, not the quality of the work. It sits at the top of the scale.

title.note: It names the tree rings, the 2,000 years and the finding, limits it to Northern Hemisphere summers and says 'suggest' rather than claiming proof.

access.note: Only some people can read it: the journal version needs a university login and a copy from the authors turns up only by searching university archives.

source.note: It appeared in one of the most widely cited science journals, where three climate scientists and a statistics expert reviewed it.

theory.note: It uses methods from earlier studies that match ring widths to thermometer readings and fills a clear gap, since earlier records covered only a few centuries or regions.

methods.note: It combines 2,860 tree-ring records from Europe and Asia using models that allow for gaps, unusual values and uncertainty, with all records and code in a public archive.

conclusion.note: The authors give margins of error and say the result covers only Northern Hemisphere summers in the regions studied, so they claim no more than the data show.

title: How Bitcoin adoption steadied a developing nation's economy
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can download it, and it is shared widely on a forum for fans of cryptocurrency (digital money such as Bitcoin).
overview: The paper draws on claims by cryptocurrency supporters that Bitcoin protects a country's money from losing value. It does not discuss economists' research on inflation (rising prices). It asks whether an economy steadied after the country made Bitcoin official money.
methods: The author compared N=6 monthly figures for prices and the currency's value: three before the switch, three after. Global oil prices, which also affect this economy, changed sharply in those months but are left out. Data availability: The paper links to some public charts but shares no raw data.
conclusion: The author concludes that Bitcoin alone made prices and the currency steadier. The paper recommends that other developing nations adopt Bitcoin too.
source: The author posted it on a public preprint server (where papers are shared before peer review). No economists have reviewed it yet.

feedback.summary: Six monthly figures, oil prices left out and no raw data cannot show that Bitcoin alone steadied an economy. Yet the paper says so and ignores research on inflation. Free access, a title without hype words and its status as a preprint, which may yet be peer reviewed, keep it just off the bottom of the scale.

title.note: It uses no hype words, but 'steadied' claims Bitcoin caused the change and leaves out that only three months either side of the switch were compared.

access.note: Anyone can download it free online, though Access is about how open a paper is, not whether its findings are right.

source.note: It is a preprint on a public server, so it may still be peer reviewed, but no economist has checked it yet and the fan forum adds no checks.

theory.note: It relies on claims by cryptocurrency supporters and does not discuss economists' research on inflation (rising prices), so it ignores what is already known.

methods.note: Six monthly figures, three before and three after the switch, are far too few, oil prices that also changed sharply are left out and no raw data are shared.

conclusion.note: Crediting Bitcoin alone while oil prices also changed sharply confuses a link in time with a cause, yet the paper urges other developing nations to adopt Bitcoin too.

title: Vertical farms are greener, using less land and water to grow lettuce
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can download the full paper and appendix.
overview: Many farm studies have used life-cycle assessment (adding up environmental costs over a product's whole life). This study applies it in the same way to lettuce from vertical farms (crops stacked indoors under lamps) and from fields.
methods: The team compared N=3 vertical farms with average published figures for field-grown lettuce. They weighed electricity for lights and heating against diesel for tractors and lorries. Data availability: Every assumption and input figure is in the appendix.
conclusion: The authors report a trade-off: vertical farms used far less land and water but much more electricity. Whether they release less carbon depends on how local electricity is made. The authors note that three farms may not represent all vertical farms.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed sustainable farming journal run by a large scientific society. A government research council funded it.

feedback.summary: Free access, a peer-reviewed society journal, every input figure in the appendix and an honest conclusion about the trade-off are clear strengths. But it compares only three vertical farms with average field figures and applies a familiar method in the usual way. Its title leaves out the extra electricity use. It sits just above the middle of the scale.

title.note: It reports the land and water savings, but 'greener' leaves out the much higher electricity use, which makes any carbon saving depend on how local electricity is made.

access.note: Anyone can download the full paper and its appendix free online, so readers can check every figure for themselves.

source.note: It appeared in a peer-reviewed farming journal run by a large scientific society, with funding from a government research council.

theory.note: Life-cycle assessment (adding up a product's environmental costs) is sound and widely used, but this study applies it in the usual way without a new argument.

methods.note: Every assumption and input figure is shared in the appendix, but comparing just three vertical farms with average published field figures is a narrow basis.

conclusion.note: It reports a real trade-off, says the carbon result depends on how local electricity is made and admits that three farms may not represent all vertical farms.

title: Tracked phone use after 10 pm linked to shorter, poorer sleep in 500 teenagers
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £36. No free copy is available.
overview: Earlier surveys linked late phone use to poor sleep, but people had to remember their own habits. Mistakes in what people remember are called recall bias. This study measures phone use and sleep directly.
methods: For two weeks, an app logged when N=500 teenagers used their phones and a wrist sensor tracked their sleep (actigraphy). The analysis plan was preregistered. Data availability: Summary data are free in a public online archive; individual records stay private to protect the teenagers.
conclusion: Teenagers who used their phones more after 10 pm slept less and less well, a statistically significant link. The authors say this does not prove phones cause poor sleep; stress, for example, might affect both.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed general medical journal that accepts about one paper in twenty. A statistics expert checks every paper.

feedback.summary: Phone use and sleep were tracked directly in 500 teenagers and the analysis plan was preregistered. The selective journal checks every paper's statistics and the conclusion does not claim cause. Only the paywall holds it back from the top of the scale. At £36 with no free copy, few readers can check the work for themselves.

title.note: It names the tracking, the 500 teenagers and the 10 pm cut-off and says 'linked to', so it reports a link without claiming phones cause poor sleep.

access.note: At £36 with no free copy, almost no one can read the full paper without paying, although Access is about openness, not whether findings are correct.

source.note: It appeared in a peer-reviewed medical journal that accepts about one paper in twenty and has a statistics expert check every paper.

theory.note: It fills a clear gap: earlier surveys relied on people remembering their own habits (recall bias), so this study measures phone use and sleep directly.

methods.note: An app and a wrist sensor tracked 500 teenagers for two weeks, with a preregistered analysis plan, public summary data and individual records withheld to protect them.

conclusion.note: It reports a statistically significant link but says this does not prove phones cause poor sleep, since stress, for example, might affect both.

title: Breakthrough cream reverses skin ageing in just 12 weeks
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £39. The authors do not share copies.
overview: Peptides (small protein pieces) may help skin make collagen, the protein that keeps skin firm. The trial asks whether a peptide cream makes skin look younger. It does not discuss earlier studies that doubt peptides can pass through the skin's outer layer.
methods: Over 12 weeks, N=120 women aged 40 to 60 used the cream twice daily, with no placebo cream. The women rated their own skin; researchers rated before-and-after photos, knowing which was which. Data availability: The company keeps the raw data; only a summary is published.
conclusion: On average, the women said their skin looked four years younger. Wrinkle depth was not measured. The authors state the cream turns back the signs of skin ageing.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed skin medicine journal that mostly prints trials funded by cosmetics companies. The cream's maker funded this one.

feedback.summary: There was no placebo cream, researchers rated photos knowing which came first, the maker keeps the raw data and wrinkle depth was not measured. Yet the title and conclusion say the cream reverses ageing. The paper also costs £39 to read. Peer review and a real question about peptides keep it just off the bottom of the scale.

title.note: 'Breakthrough' is a hype word and 'reverses skin ageing' promises a real physical change, yet the trial never measured wrinkle depth.

access.note: The paper costs £39 and the authors do not share copies, so almost no one can read it without paying.

source.note: It was peer reviewed, but the journal mostly prints trials funded by cosmetics companies and the cream's maker paid for this one, so that check reassures less.

theory.note: It builds on the idea that peptides (small protein pieces) may help skin make collagen, but ignores earlier studies that doubt peptides can pass the skin's outer layer.

methods.note: Self-ratings, no placebo cream, photo raters who knew which pictures came first and raw data kept by the maker outweigh a fair-sized sample of 120 women.

conclusion.note: Claiming the cream turns back skin ageing treats the women's sense that they looked four years younger as fact, though wrinkle depth was never measured.

title: Systematic review of 38 trials: mindfulness brings small to moderate chronic pain relief
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the full review and download its data.
overview: Many randomised controlled trials have tested mindfulness (training attention on the present moment) for chronic (long-lasting) pain, with mixed results. This review combines them, drawing on research into how the brain handles pain.
methods: Following a preregistered plan, the team found 38 suitable trials with N=3,540 participants and combined them in a meta-analysis. Two reviewers working separately checked each trial for bias. Data availability: All extracted data and code are free online.
conclusion: The authors report a small to moderate drop in pain (effect size 0.33) that varied widely between trials. Mindfulness helped some kinds of pain more than others. They say it can support medical treatment but not replace it.
source: Published in a library of health reviews run by an international non-profit research network. Each review's plan and final text are peer reviewed.

feedback.summary: It is free to read and comes from a peer-reviewed library of health reviews. It combines 38 trials with 3,540 people under a preregistered plan, with two reviewers checking each trial for bias. All data and code are open and the conclusion reports how widely results varied. Strong on every criterion, it sits at the top of the scale.

title.note: It names the design, the 38 trials and the condition and says the relief was small to moderate, with no promise of a cure.

access.note: Anyone can read the full review and download its data free online, so readers can check exactly how it was done.

source.note: It appeared in a library of health reviews run by an international non-profit network, where each review's plan and final text are peer reviewed.

theory.note: It brings together many randomised controlled trials with mixed results to answer one clear question, drawing on research into how the brain handles pain.

methods.note: A preregistered meta-analysis of 38 trials with 3,540 people, separate bias checks by two reviewers and all extracted data and code free online make this careful, open work.

conclusion.note: It reports a small to moderate drop in pain that varied widely, notes some kinds of pain improved more and says mindfulness can support medical treatment but not replace it.

title: Magnet-treated water eased symptoms in adults with long-term illness, eight-week trial finds
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can download the full paper and its data.
overview: Sellers of water magnets say magnets arrange water molecules into 'structured' clusters that cells absorb more easily. Chemistry research shows such clusters last under a billionth of a second; the paper does not mention this. It asks whether structured water eases diabetes, arthritis or depression.
methods: The first 40 of N=80 volunteers to sign up drank structured water (tap water passed between magnets); the rest drank tap water. Everyone knew which water they had and rated their own symptoms on a questionnaire. Data availability: The full dataset is free with the paper.
conclusion: The structured water group reported fewer symptoms. The authors say structured water treats long-term illness and advise patients to drink it daily.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed alternative medicine journal run by a therapists' association. Most of its reviewers offer the therapies it covers.

feedback.summary: Free access to the full paper and data, plus a tap-water comparison group, keeps it just off the bottom. But its idea clashes with chemistry the paper leaves out. The first to sign up got magnet-treated water and everyone rated their own symptoms knowing which water they had. Yet the authors say it treats long-term illness.

title.note: It uses no hype words, but 'eased symptoms' leaves out that people rated their own symptoms while knowing which water they drank.

access.note: Anyone can download the full paper and its data free online, though being easy to read says nothing about whether the findings are correct.

source.note: It is peer reviewed, but the journal is run by a therapists' association and most reviewers offer the therapies it covers, so they may favour positive results.

theory.note: It rests on 'structured' water clusters, but chemistry research shows such clusters last under a billionth of a second, which the paper never mentions.

methods.note: Eighty volunteers, a tap-water group and free data are a fair base, but the first to sign up got magnet-treated water and people rated their own symptoms knowing their group.

conclusion.note: Self-rated symptoms from people who knew which water they drank cannot show the water treats illness, yet the authors claim it does and advise patients to drink it daily.

title: Breakthrough drug halts memory loss in Alzheimer's patients
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £45. No free copy is available.
overview: Alzheimer's is linked to amyloid-beta plaques (protein clumps in the brain). This trial asks whether a drug that clears them slows memory loss. Experts disagree about what small changes on its memory score mean.
methods: The trial randomly gave N=1,800 people the drug or a placebo for 18 months; neither patients nor doctors knew which. By the end 32% had dropped out, and some comparisons were added after the results were in. Data availability: Summary figures are published; full data are on request.
conclusion: The authors call the 27% slower decline on this score, compared with placebo, a clear benefit. They note the drug restored no lost abilities and caused brain swelling in 13% of patients. The dropouts are not discussed.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed medical journal that accepts one paper in twenty. The drug's maker paid for the whole trial.

feedback.summary: Its main strength is a large trial in which chance decided who got the drug or a placebo (dummy treatment). Neither patients nor doctors knew which. But the drug's maker paid for it all, 32% dropped out and comparisons were added after the results. With a £45 paywall and a hype title, it sits in the middle of the scale.

title.note: 'Breakthrough' is a hype word, and 'halts memory loss' goes far beyond a slower decline on one memory score with no lost abilities restored.

access.note: At £45 with no free copy, almost no one can read the full paper without paying, so few readers can check the trial for themselves.

source.note: The medical journal is peer reviewed and accepts one paper in twenty, but the drug's maker paid for the whole trial, so the maker had a stake in the result.

theory.note: It builds on the known link between amyloid plaques (protein clumps) and Alzheimer's, but experts disagree about what small changes on its memory score mean.

methods.note: A randomised, double-blind trial of 1,800 people is a strong design, but 32% dropped out, comparisons were added after the results and full data are only on request.

conclusion.note: The authors report that no lost abilities came back and 13% had brain swelling, but call a 27% slower decline a clear benefit and never discuss the dropouts.

title: Income gaps linked to poorer health in 40-year observational study of 50 countries
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the full paper.
overview: Earlier studies linked bigger income gaps to poorer health, but critics said poverty might explain this. This study asks whether the link remains after allowing for each country's wealth.
methods: Following a preregistered plan, the team analysed 40 years of figures for N=50 countries, allowing for wealth, health spending and education. About 15% of health figures were missing; the team estimated them and checked whether this changed the results. Data availability: All data and code are free in a public archive.
conclusion: Countries with wider income gaps had lower life expectancy, more infant deaths and mental illness, even allowing for wealth. The authors stress that observational data cannot prove cause. They add that the estimated figures may affect the results.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed public health journal that accepts one paper in twelve. A statistics specialist checks every paper.

feedback.summary: This is excellent work on every criterion. It is free to read and appears in a selective journal with statistics checks. It tests a known criticism, follows a plan fixed in advance and shares its data and code. Its conclusion says plainly what observational data cannot prove. Naming limits such as the estimated figures counts in its favour.

title.note: It states the design, the 40 years and the 50 countries and says 'linked', which claims a link rather than a cause, with no hype words.

access.note: Anyone can read the full paper free online, so everyone can check the work for themselves.

source.note: It appears in a peer-reviewed public health journal that accepts one paper in twelve, where a statistics specialist checks every paper.

theory.note: It fills a clear gap by testing whether the earlier link between income gaps and health survives the critics' point that poverty might explain it.

methods.note: A preregistered plan (fixed in advance), 40 years of figures from 50 countries, checks on the 15% of estimated figures and free data and code make this careful, open work.

conclusion.note: It reports wider income gaps alongside poorer health even allowing for wealth, stresses that observational data cannot prove cause and warns the estimated figures may affect results.

title: Proven: new energy drink makes athletes perform 35% better
access: Only a two-page summary is on the company's website. The full report is confidential.
overview: Decades of sports research show caffeine's benefits level off above a moderate dose and differ between people. The report does not mention this. It credits the drink's caffeine and taurine (a common energy drink ingredient) with 'unlocking hidden energy'.
methods: The company gave N=20 athletes the energy drink or water and timed them on eight speed and stamina tests. The athletes knew which drink they had, and the company owned the timing equipment. Data availability: The data are private.
conclusion: The report's headline says the drink improves performance by 35%, a figure from one sprint test. Across all eight tests the average gain was 2%, about as much as athletes' results vary day to day.
source: A white paper (a report a company publishes itself) from the drink maker's own laboratory. Its lead author is the company's head of marketing.

feedback.summary: The drink maker's head of marketing led this report and the full text is confidential. The 20 athletes knew which drink they had. The 35% headline comes from one sprint test, while the average gain was 2%. Only the timed comparison with water, a real if limited test, keeps it just above the very bottom.

title.note: 'Proven' is a hype word, and '35% better' turns one sprint test into a claim about performance in general, when the average gain was 2%.

access.note: Only a two-page summary is public and the full report is confidential, so almost no one can check how the tests were run.

source.note: It is a white paper the drink maker published itself, from its own laboratory and led by its head of marketing, so the seller judged its own product.

theory.note: It credits caffeine and taurine with 'unlocking hidden energy' and ignores decades of research showing caffeine's benefits level off and differ between people.

methods.note: Only 20 athletes took part, they knew which drink they had, the company owned the timing equipment and the data are private.

conclusion.note: Headlining a 35% gain from one sprint test, when the average across all eight was 2% and within normal day-to-day ups and downs, is cherry-picking.

title: Leaked papers suggest vaccine injuries are under-reported
access: Free to everyone online: the 40-page report can be downloaded with no sign-up.
overview: The report uses a government database where anyone can log a health problem after a vaccine, without checks. The database warns that an entry does not show the vaccine caused the problem. The report asks whether officials hide the true number of injuries.
methods: There is no new research: the report quotes single sentences from leaked regulatory papers without the text around them. It counts every database entry as an injury and does not check how often the same illnesses happen without vaccines. Data availability: None.
conclusion: According to the author, vaccines have injured far more people than official figures show, and regulators are hiding this.
source: The report was posted on a website that sells supplements to 'protect against vaccine damage' and calls COVID-19 a hoax. The author is anonymous and no one outside the website checked it.

feedback.summary: There is no new research here. An anonymous report on a website selling supplements against 'vaccine damage' quotes leaked papers out of context. It also counts every unchecked database entry as an injury. A free download and a calm-sounding title cannot make up for that, so it sits at the bottom of the scale.

title.note: It sounds measured, with no hype words, but 'leaked papers suggest' hints at secret evidence and leaves out that the report only quotes single sentences out of context.

access.note: Anyone can download the full 40-page report free with no sign-up, though easy access says nothing about whether its claims are true.

source.note: It was posted anonymously on a website that sells supplements against 'vaccine damage' and calls COVID-19 a hoax; no one outside the website checked it.

theory.note: It treats an unchecked database, where anyone can log a health problem after a vaccine, as a count of injuries, despite the database's own warning.

methods.note: There is no new research: it quotes single sentences from leaked papers, counts every entry as an injury, never checks how often these illnesses happen anyway and shares no data.

conclusion.note: The claim of far more injuries and a cover-up rests on entries showing only what came after a vaccine, not what it caused.

title: Mediterranean diet cuts dementia risk by almost a quarter
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £39. No free copy is available.
overview: A Mediterranean diet is rich in vegetables, fish and olive oil. Earlier studies linked it to slower memory decline, but most lasted under ten years. This study looks for a link with dementia over 25 years.
methods: This cohort study followed N=8,000 adults for 25 years, allowing for education, exercise, smoking and APOE4 (a gene linked to dementia). Everyone had the same dementia checks, but people filled in a tested diet questionnaire only once, at the start. Data availability: Group totals are in an appendix; individual data are on request.
conclusion: People who followed the diet most closely had 23% less dementia than those who followed it least. The authors stress this is a link, not proof: healthier people may also choose healthier diets.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed general medicine journal whose impact factor is about average for medical journals.

feedback.summary: Following 8,000 adults for 25 years fills a gap left by shorter studies. The conclusion also calls the result a link, not proof. These strengths outweigh its limits. Diet was asked about only once, individual data are on request, the paper costs £39 and the title says the diet 'cuts' risk.

title.note: It reports the finding without hype words, but 'cuts dementia risk' turns a link into a cause, which the authors themselves avoid.

access.note: At £39 with no free copy, almost no one can read the full paper without paying, although that says nothing about whether the findings are correct.

source.note: It appeared in a peer-reviewed general medicine journal, but one whose impact factor (how often its papers are cited) is only about average for medical journals.

theory.note: It fills a clear gap: earlier studies linked the diet to slower memory decline but mostly lasted under ten years, so this one follows people for 25 years.

methods.note: It follows 8,000 adults for 25 years and allows for smoking and a gene linked to dementia, but diet was recorded only once and individual data are on request.

conclusion.note: It reports 23% less dementia among those who followed the diet most closely and stresses this is a link, not proof, since healthier people may choose healthier diets.

title: Daily reading to babies improved language at age 3 in a randomised trial, but gains shrank by age 5
access: Not free to everyone: the paper needs a university library login.
overview: Children in lower-income homes often hear fewer words before school, which is linked to later reading. Few trials have tested whether daily reading to babies helps their language.
methods: Forty health centres serving N=600 families were randomly split: half gave free books and reading-aloud training, half the usual check-ups. Testers did not know each child's group, and outcomes were preregistered. Data availability: Anonymised data and code are free in a public online archive.
conclusion: Children in the reading group had larger vocabularies and better grammar at age 3, especially in lower-income families. By age 5 the difference had shrunk. The authors say reading alone will not close gaps in school success.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed child development journal that accepts about one paper in ten. It also publishes replications (repeat studies).

feedback.summary: This is excellent work. Forty health centres were split by chance and testers did not know each child's group. Outcomes were fixed in advance, data and code are open and the conclusion reports the gains shrinking by age 5. The only weakness, a university login, limits who can read it, not how good it is.

title.note: It names the design and the finding at age 3 and adds the key limit that the gains had shrunk by age 5, with no hype.

access.note: Only some people can read it, because the paper needs a university library login, though the anonymised data and code are free to all.

source.note: It appears in a peer-reviewed child development journal that accepts about one paper in ten and also publishes replications (repeat studies).

theory.note: It fills a clear gap: children in lower-income homes often hear fewer words before school, but few trials have tested whether daily reading helps.

methods.note: Randomly splitting 40 health centres serving 600 families, with testers who did not know each child's group, preregistered outcomes and open data and code, is careful, open work.

conclusion.note: It reports gains at age 3, especially in lower-income families, says the difference had shrunk by age 5 and warns reading alone will not close school gaps.

title: Review raises questions about 5G networks and cancer, autism and infertility
access: Free to everyone online: the article is on a public website and widely shared on social media.
overview: The article says 5G signals damage DNA in the same way as X-rays. X-rays are ionising radiation: they carry enough energy to break bonds in DNA. 5G radio waves carry far less energy and cannot do this, which the article does not mention.
methods: The article reports no research of its own. It quotes unnamed 'scientists' and studies of high doses of X-rays, none of them about mobile networks. Data availability: None.
conclusion: The article claims that 5G networks cause cancer, autism and infertility. It urges readers to switch off their phones at night and to oppose new phone masts.
source: The website names no editors and has no peer review. Its other articles say the Earth is flat. The author is named but lists no science training.

feedback.summary: There is no research here, just an article on a website with no named editors or peer review. The site's other articles say the Earth is flat. It claims 5G damages DNA like X-rays, but radio waves carry far too little energy. A free link and a calm title do not change that, so it sits at the bottom.

title.note: It uses no hype words, but 'review raises questions' suggests a careful look at evidence, when the article reports no research and simply claims harm.

access.note: Anyone can read it free on a public website, but being widely shared on social media says nothing about whether it is true.

source.note: The website names no editors, has no peer review and runs articles saying the Earth is flat; the named author lists no science training.

theory.note: It says 5G damages DNA like X-rays, ignoring that 5G radio waves carry far less energy than X-rays and cannot break bonds in DNA.

methods.note: It reports no research of its own and shares no data, only quotes from unnamed 'scientists' and studies of high X-ray doses unrelated to mobile networks.

conclusion.note: The article blames 5G for cancer, autism and infertility and urges readers to oppose phone masts, with no evidence beyond a mix-up of radio waves and X-rays.

title: Lifesaving AI breakthrough spots deadly pancreatic cancer early from routine blood tests
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the paper and its code.
overview: Pancreatic cancer is usually found too late to treat well. Earlier work found small blood-test changes months before diagnosis. This study asks whether machine learning (software that learns from examples) can spot them.
methods: The program learned from blood-test records of N=2,000 people: 500 later diagnosed and 1,500 similar people without cancer. It was then tested on records of 400 patients from different hospitals. Data availability: The code is free online; patient data need an ethics review of 6 to 12 months.
conclusion: The program sorted 92% of the test group correctly. The authors say it needs testing in real clinics first: false alarms would cause worry and needless tests.
source: It appeared in a widely cited, peer-reviewed medical AI journal that only accepts tools tested on a separate group of patients. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

feedback.summary: Free access, a demanding peer-reviewed journal, a clear medical gap, testing on 400 patients from other hospitals, free code and a cautious conclusion put this near the top of the scale. Only the title lets it down: 'Lifesaving AI breakthrough' promises lives saved, while the authors say the program still needs testing in clinics.

title.note: 'Lifesaving' and 'breakthrough' are hype words: the program was tested only on existing blood-test records and the authors say it still needs testing in real clinics.

access.note: Anyone can read the full paper and its code free online, so every reader can see how the program was built and tested.

source.note: It appeared in a widely cited, peer-reviewed journal that accepts only tools tested on a separate group of patients, with no conflicts of interest declared.

theory.note: It fills a clear gap for a cancer usually found too late, building on earlier work that found small blood-test changes months before diagnosis.

methods.note: Learning from 500 people later diagnosed and 1,500 similar people without cancer, then testing on 400 patients from other hospitals, is thorough, though patient data need months of ethics review.

conclusion.note: The authors report that 92% were sorted correctly but say the program needs testing in real clinics first, warning that false alarms would cause worry and needless tests.

title: Alkaline diet cure: eat the right foods and your blood will starve cancer
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can download the e-book from the author's website.
overview: The e-book says meat and coffee make blood acidic and feed cancer, while 'alkaline' foods stop it. Medical textbooks explain that the lungs and kidneys keep blood pH (acidity) between 7.35 and 7.45, whatever we eat. The e-book cites none of this.
methods: The only evidence is the author's own urine test strips, which changed colour after a glass of lemon water. Urine pH changes with diet, but blood pH does not. Data availability: None.
conclusion: The author concludes that alkaline foods 'starve' cancer and prevent it. Readers are told to test their urine daily and drink alkaline water.
source: The e-book was self-published by a wellness coach with no medical or science training, and no one else checked it. Each chapter links to the author's shop, which sells £899 alkaline water machines.

feedback.summary: A wellness coach who sells £899 water machines self-published this e-book and nobody checked it. Its idea ignores how the lungs and kidneys keep blood pH steady, while its only evidence is the author's own urine strips. Being free to read cannot make up for that, so it sits at the bottom of the scale.

title.note: 'Cure' is a hype word and 'your blood will starve cancer' promises far more than one person's urine strips could show.

access.note: Anyone can download the e-book free from the author's website, though Access is about how open a work is, not whether its claims are true.

source.note: A wellness coach with no medical or science training self-published it, nobody else checked it and every chapter links to the author's shop selling £899 water machines.

theory.note: It ignores what medical textbooks explain: the lungs and kidneys keep blood pH between 7.35 and 7.45 whatever we eat, so food cannot make blood acidic.

methods.note: The only evidence is the author's urine strips changing colour after lemon water, but urine tests cannot show blood pH, no one else was tested and no data are shared.

conclusion.note: Claiming that alkaline foods starve and prevent cancer rests on urine strips alone, yet readers are told to test their urine daily and drink alkaline water.

title: One-off survey of adults in 50 cities links nearby green space with less anxiety and depression
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £37. No free copy is available.
overview: Environmental psychology suggests that time in nature lowers stress. Many earlier surveys have already linked parks with better mental health. This study asks whether the same link appears across 50 cities.
methods: In this cross-sectional study, N=15,000 adults in 50 cities answered one survey about anxiety and depression. Satellite images measured the greenery within 1 km of each home. Data availability: Only summary tables are shared.
conclusion: People with more greenery nearby reported less anxiety and depression. The authors call this a link, not proof: income could explain both, or calmer people may choose homes near parks. They suggest experiments to test cause and effect.
