source: It appeared in a peer-reviewed environmental health journal that accepts about half the papers it receives. Its papers are cited less than those in the field's most-cited journals.

feedback.summary: A large survey with a precise title and a careful 'link, not proof' conclusion lifts this study. But it adds little to earlier surveys of the same link, asks people only once, shares only summary tables and costs £37 to read in a less-cited journal. Its strengths and limits balance out, putting it in the middle of the scale.

title.note: It names the one-off survey, the adults and the 50 cities and says 'links', so readers know it shows a connection, not a cause.

access.note: Reading it costs £37 with no free copy, so almost no one can check it without paying, though price says nothing about quality.

source.note: Peer review is a real check, but this journal accepts about half the papers it receives and is cited less than the field's most-cited journals.

theory.note: It rests on a sound idea from environmental psychology, but many surveys already link parks with better mental health, so a 50-city check fills no clear gap.

methods.note: Surveying 15,000 adults and measuring greenery from satellite images are strengths, but a one-off survey cannot show cause and only summary tables are shared.

conclusion.note: The authors call it a link, not proof, name income and calmer people choosing homes near parks as other explanations and suggest experiments to test cause.

title: Super yogurt boosts your immune system by 80%, scientists prove
access: Only a one-page press release describes the study. The full study is unpublished, and requests for it get no reply.
overview: Probiotics are live bacteria meant to benefit health, and some research suggests certain gut bacteria affect parts of the immune system. The release asks whether the company's own types of bacteria improve 'immune function', without saying which part it means.
methods: Staff measured one antibody in saliva, called IgA, in N=30 people before and after two weeks of eating the yogurt. There was no comparison group and no plan published in advance. Data availability: None.
conclusion: The release says the yogurt 'boosts immunity by 80%'. This is the average rise in IgA, which also varies from day to day. The study did not measure infections or any other health outcome.
source: The yogurt's maker put out the press release. Company staff ran the study, and no one outside the company checked it.

feedback.summary: This is a company press release, not a published study. Staff tested 30 people for two weeks with no comparison group, nobody can read the full study and the '80%' is the average rise in one antibody that varies from day to day. Asking whether probiotics affect immunity is a fair question, which keeps it just off the bottom.

title.note: 'Super yogurt', '80%' and 'scientists prove' are hype, since staff measured one antibody in 30 people and checked no health outcome at all.

access.note: Only a one-page press release is available: the full study is unpublished and requests for it get no reply, so no one can check it.

source.note: The yogurt's maker put out the release, its own staff ran the study and no one outside the company checked it.

theory.note: Some research suggests gut bacteria affect parts of the immune system, but the release never says which part of 'immune function' it means.

methods.note: Thirty people measured before and after two weeks, with no comparison group, no plan published in advance and no data shared, cannot show the yogurt did anything.

conclusion.note: Saying the yogurt 'boosts immunity by 80%' turns the average rise in one saliva antibody, which varies day to day, into a health claim the study never tested.

title: Psilocybin given with therapy eased hard-to-treat depression in a double-blind trial of 100 adults
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the trial report.
overview: Psilocybin, the active chemical in 'magic mushrooms', acts like serotonin (a chemical messenger in the brain). Small earlier studies suggested it eases depression alongside therapy. This trial tests it in adults not helped by two or more antidepressants.
methods: The preregistered trial randomly gave N=100 adults psilocybin or a placebo, with the same therapy for both. Patients and the independent assessors did not know who got which, and follow-up lasted six months. Data availability: Anonymised data need an ethics application, which takes several months.
conclusion: Depression scores fell more with psilocybin than with placebo. The authors note that patients also had intensive therapy, some relapsed and long-term safety is unknown.
source: It appeared in a peer-reviewed psychiatry journal that rejects nine in ten papers and requires trials to be preregistered. The authors declare no drug company funding.

feedback.summary: Chance decided who got psilocybin or a placebo in this preregistered trial and neither patients nor assessors knew which. It is free to read in a selective journal and the authors name relapses and unknown long-term safety. Strong on every criterion, it sits at the top of the scale, though the data take months to obtain.

title.note: It names the therapy given alongside the drug, the double-blind design and the 100 adults with hard-to-treat depression, saying 'eased' rather than 'cured'.

access.note: Anyone can read the full trial report free online, so every reader can check how the trial was run.

source.note: It appeared in a peer-reviewed psychiatry journal that rejects nine in ten papers and requires preregistration, with no drug company funding declared.

theory.note: Small earlier studies suggested psilocybin eases depression, so this larger trial is a needed check (a replication) in adults not helped by two or more antidepressants.

methods.note: A preregistered, double-blind trial randomly giving 100 adults psilocybin or a placebo with the same therapy, followed for six months, is careful work, though data need an ethics application.

conclusion.note: The authors report that scores fell more with psilocybin but note the intensive therapy, some relapses and unknown long-term safety, claiming no more than the trial shows.

title: Industry panel's narrative review of 45 studies finds no health risks from genetically modified crops
access: Free to everyone online: the full report is on its publisher's website.
overview: Large independent reviews have found no clear health risk from eating GM crops. Other research raises concerns about weedkiller use and wildlife. The report sets out to summarise research on GM crop safety rather than test anything new.
methods: This is a narrative review: the panel chose N=45 studies to discuss, with no search plan set in advance. All 45 report no harm, and none of the research on weedkiller use or wildlife is included. Data availability: None.
conclusion: The panel concludes that GM crops pose no risk to health or the environment. It calls research raising concerns 'anti-science' without discussing its findings.
source: The report comes from an industry group that speaks for biotech companies. All six authors work for companies selling genetically modified (GM) seeds, and no outside experts checked it.

feedback.summary: An accurate title and free access are its main strengths. But six authors from companies selling GM seeds picked 45 studies with no search plan, all reporting no harm. They left out research on weedkiller use and wildlife yet still declared GM crops safe for the environment. That one-sided review keeps it near the bottom of the scale.

title.note: It says plainly that this is an industry panel's narrative review of 45 studies, so readers can see who wrote it and what kind of work it is.

access.note: Anyone can read the full report free on its publisher's website, though Access is about how open a work is, not whether it is balanced.

source.note: An industry group for biotech companies published it, all six authors work for firms selling GM seeds and no outside experts checked it.

theory.note: It starts from large independent reviews that found no clear health risk, but only sets out to summarise research rather than build a new argument.

methods.note: With no search plan, the panel picked 45 studies that all report no harm and left out research on weedkiller use and wildlife, which is cherry-picking.

conclusion.note: It claims GM crops pose no risk to the environment without reviewing any wildlife research and calls research raising concerns 'anti-science' without discussing what it found.

title: Seas will rise by about a metre by 2100, climate study finds
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the paper and download all results and code.
overview: Seas rise as warming water expands and land ice melts, which physicists have long understood. Earlier projections handled ice sheets (huge ice layers on Greenland and Antarctica) only roughly. This study adds newer research on how ice sheets break up.
methods: Following a preregistered plan, the team compared N=30 climate models, giving the uncertainty of every estimate. They checked the models against satellite, tide-gauge (coastal sea-level) and past-climate records. Data availability: All model outputs and code are free in public archives.
conclusion: Under high emissions, the models project a rise of 0.6 to 1.1 metres by 2100, varying by region. The authors stress this is a model range, with ice sheets the biggest unknown.
source: It appeared in a peer-reviewed earth science journal whose reviewers rerun the code to check they get the same results.

feedback.summary: It is free to read, reviewers rerun its code and it fills a clear gap on ice sheets. It compares 30 models under a preregistered plan and checks them against real records. The conclusion gives a range. Only the title falls short by turning that range into a firm forecast, so it stays at the top of the scale.

title.note: It gives the main finding without hype words, but 'will rise by about a metre' sounds certain and leaves out that this is a model range under high emissions.

access.note: Anyone can read the paper free online and download all its results and code, so others can check the work for themselves.

source.note: It appeared in a peer-reviewed earth science journal whose reviewers rerun the code to check they get the same results, a demanding level of checking.

theory.note: It builds on long-understood physics of warming water and melting ice and fills a clear gap, since earlier projections handled ice sheets only roughly.

methods.note: The team followed a preregistered plan, compared 30 models, gave the uncertainty of each estimate, checked the models against real records and made all outputs and code public.

conclusion.note: The authors give a range of 0.6 to 1.1 metres under high emissions, note that it varies by region and name ice sheets as the biggest unknown.

title: Shocking lab results expose mind-control chemicals in chemtrails
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the blog post.
overview: The post says the white trails behind aircraft are 'chemtrails': chemicals sprayed to control minds. It does not mention that contrails (condensation trails) are ice crystals formed when hot, wet engine exhaust meets cold air.
methods: An unnamed lab tested one jar of rainwater, the author says, with no record of who handled it. The post shows blurry photos of aircraft trails and a results sheet with the lab's name blacked out. Data availability: None.
conclusion: The post says the aluminium and barium on the results sheet prove that governments spray mind-control chemicals. Both metals are common in soil and dust, and small amounts turn up in ordinary rainwater.
source: The blog gives no author name, qualifications or contact details. Nothing is checked before posting, and other posts say a secret group runs world governments.

feedback.summary: An anonymous blog that checks nothing rests its mind-control claim on one jar of rainwater, tested by an unnamed lab with no record of who handled it. It ignores how contrails form, while the metals it reports turn up in ordinary rainwater. Free access is its only strength and cannot lift it off the bottom of the scale.

title.note: 'Shocking' and 'expose' are hype words, while 'mind-control chemicals' promises far more than one jar of rainwater from an unnamed lab could show.

access.note: Anyone can read the blog post free, though Access is about how open a work is, not whether its claims are true.

source.note: The blog names no author, qualifications or contact details, checks nothing before posting and claims elsewhere that a secret group runs world governments.

theory.note: It never mentions that contrails are ice crystals formed when hot, wet engine exhaust meets cold air, so it ignores basic science about aircraft trails.

methods.note: One jar of rainwater, an unnamed lab, no record of who handled it and a results sheet with the lab's name blacked out give nothing anyone could check.

conclusion.note: Aluminium and barium are common in soil and dust and turn up in ordinary rainwater, so finding them cannot show anyone sprays mind-control chemicals.

title: Real-world study of 5,000 people finds PrEP stops HIV infection
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the paper.
overview: PrEP, most often a daily pill, prevents infection with HIV (the virus that causes AIDS). Earlier randomised controlled trials found it works when taken as prescribed. This study asks how well it works in everyday life.
methods: This cohort study followed N=5,000 people at high risk of HIV, using blood tests to check they took PrEP. They were compared with similar patients in past clinic records (historical controls), not a group chosen by chance. Data availability: On request from the authors.
conclusion: The authors report almost complete protection with daily use, falling sharply with missed doses. They note PrEP does not prevent other sexually transmitted infections. Only an extra online file mentions that the past patients may have differed in other ways.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed infectious disease journal run by a large medical society. A government health agency funded the study.

feedback.summary: Free access, a peer-reviewed society journal, a real-world test of earlier trials and blood tests confirming pill use in 5,000 people stand out. It falls just short of the top because users were compared with past patients and only an extra file admits the groups may have differed. Data come only on request and the title leaves out daily use.

title.note: It names the real-world setting and sample size without hype words, but 'stops HIV infection' leaves out that protection depended on daily use and was judged against past patients.

access.note: Anyone can read the full paper free online, so every reader can check the methods and claims for themselves.

source.note: It appeared in a peer-reviewed infectious disease journal run by a large medical society, with funding from a government health agency.

theory.note: Earlier randomised trials showed PrEP works when taken as prescribed, so testing how well it works in everyday life is a needed next step.

methods.note: Checking pill use in 5,000 people with blood tests is a strength, but data are only on request and the comparison is past patients, not a group chosen by chance.

conclusion.note: It admits protection falls with missed doses and PrEP does not stop other sexually transmitted infections, but mentions only in an extra online file that past patients may have differed.

title: Turn back the clock: testosterone therapy restores youth to men over 40
access: Not free to everyone: only subscribers can read the magazine, but the author's clinic emails copies on request.
overview: Testosterone (the main male sex hormone) falls slowly in most men from about 40, as part of normal ageing. The article calls this a disease and cites no hormone research or safety studies.
methods: The author looked back at the records of N=48 clinic patients who chose to pay for testosterone. Patients said whether they 'felt better'; there was no comparison group and no long-term safety checks. Data availability: None.
conclusion: Because most patients said they felt more energetic, the author concludes that testosterone reverses ageing. It does not mention side effects such as blood clots and heart rhythm problems, whose long-term risks are unclear.
source: The article appeared in a supplement industry magazine with no peer review, beside clinic adverts. The author owns the testosterone clinic whose patients it describes.

feedback.summary: A clinic owner who sells the treatment wrote this article for a magazine with no peer review. It calls the normal fall in testosterone with age a disease and leaves out side effects. It rests on 48 paying patients saying whether they felt better, with no comparison group. Using real patient records, however weakly, keeps it just off the bottom.

title.note: 'Turn back the clock' and 'restores youth' are sales hype that promise far more than asking 48 patients whether they felt better could ever show.

access.note: Only some people can read it: the magazine is for subscribers, but the author's clinic emails copies on request.

source.note: It appeared without peer review in a supplement industry magazine beside clinic adverts, written by the owner of the clinic whose patients it describes.

theory.note: It treats the slow fall in testosterone from about 40, a normal part of ageing, as a disease and cites no hormone research or safety studies.

methods.note: Only 48 patients who chose and paid for the hormone said whether they 'felt better', with no comparison group, no long-term safety checks and no data shared.

conclusion.note: With no comparison group, patients feeling more energetic cannot show that testosterone reverses ageing, yet the author claims it does and leaves out side effects such as blood clots.

title: CRISPR gene editing corrects sickle cell disease in patient trial
access: Behind a paywall: reading the paper costs £42. No free copy is available.
overview: Sickle cell disease comes from one faulty gene that makes red blood cells stiff and curved. Lab studies showed CRISPR (a tool for editing DNA) can fix it in blood stem cells (which make new blood). This trial tests the method in patients.
methods: A single-arm trial (with no comparison group) treated N=15 adults with severe disease. Doctors followed them for two years with close safety checks. Data availability: Summary figures are in the paper; each patient's data are private.
conclusion: All 15 patients had fewer severe pain attacks and blood transfusions. The authors say no one knows how long this lasts, and the treatment is very costly. They found unintended DNA edits in two patients, who are being monitored.
source: Published in a widely read peer-reviewed medical journal. Outside experts on an independent board checked safety throughout the trial.

feedback.summary: A widely read peer-reviewed journal, an independent safety board, a clear next step from lab studies and a frank conclusion are real strengths. But only 15 patients were treated, with no comparison group. The paywall stops most readers checking it and the title says 'corrects' before anyone knows how long the benefit lasts. It sits just above the middle.

title.note: It names the method, the disease and that this was a patient trial, but 'corrects' suggests a complete, lasting fix that 15 patients over two years cannot yet show.

access.note: At £42 with no free copy, only readers who pay can see the full paper, though the price says nothing about whether the findings are correct.

source.note: It appeared in a widely read peer-reviewed medical journal, with an independent board of outside experts checking safety throughout the trial.

theory.note: It builds on lab studies showing CRISPR can fix the one faulty gene in blood-making stem cells and takes the clear next step of testing it in patients.

methods.note: Only 15 patients were treated with no comparison group and each patient's data are private, although two years of close safety checks are a strength.

conclusion.note: The authors report fewer pain attacks and transfusions but admit no one knows how long this lasts, note the high cost and disclose unintended DNA edits in two patients.

title: Eat organic and avoid all disease, 10-year study proves
access: Free to everyone online: the full report is on an organic food industry website.
overview: The report asks whether organic food protects health, starting from the idea that it prevents every kind of disease. It does not discuss genes, smoking, exercise or other causes of illness found in earlier research.
methods: For 10 years the authors tracked illnesses among N=850 organic shop customers and compared them with national figures. The customers earned more and smoked less than average, but the analysis did not take these confounding variables into account. Data availability: Not provided.
conclusion: Because the organic shoppers had fewer illnesses, the report concludes that organic food prevents all disease. It advises everyone to switch to an organic diet.
source: A report from a trade group for organic farmers and shops, which also paid for the study. The authors work for bodies that certify food as organic, and no outside experts checked it.

feedback.summary: A trade group for organic farmers and shops paid for this report, its authors work for organic certifiers and no outside experts checked it. It compares shoppers who earned more and smoked less with national figures, ignores those differences and claims organic food prevents all disease. Free access cannot make up for that, so it sits at the bottom.

title.note: 'Avoid all disease' and 'proves' promise far more than a comparison of organic shoppers with national figures could ever show.

access.note: Anyone can read the full report free on an organic food industry website, though easy access says nothing about whether its claims are true.

source.note: An organic trade group paid for the report, its authors work for organic certifiers and no outside experts checked it, so everyone involved has a stake in the result.

theory.note: It starts from the idea that organic food prevents every kind of disease and ignores earlier research on genes, smoking, exercise and other causes of illness.

methods.note: The 850 shoppers earned more and smoked less than average, yet the comparison with national figures ignored these confounding variables and no data are shared.

conclusion.note: Fewer illnesses among wealthier shoppers who smoked less cannot show the food was the cause, yet the report claims organic food prevents all disease and tells everyone to switch.

title: Three-minute walks each hour cut blood sugar rises on lab test days: crossover trial in 40 office workers
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the paper.
overview: Population studies (epidemiology) link long hours of sitting to diabetes and heart disease. This trial asks whether short walks during a day of sitting improve blood markers of these risks.
methods: In a preregistered crossover trial (each person tries both conditions), N=40 office workers spent two lab days in random order. They sat for 8 hours on one day and walked for 3 minutes each hour on the other. Data availability: All data are free online.
conclusion: Blood sugar and insulin rose less on the walking day; blood fats did not change. The authors stress this was a short lab test and do not say the breaks prevent diabetes or heart disease.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed exercise science journal run by a professional society. The journal's reviewers check each trial against its preregistered plan.

feedback.summary: Strong on every criterion, it sits at the top of the scale. It is free to read in a journal that checks trials against preregistered plans. A randomised crossover design with open data tests what population studies only linked. The title is exact and the authors stress it was a short lab test, claiming nothing about preventing disease.

title.note: It names the design, the 40 office workers, the blood sugar result and the lab setting, with no hype and no claim about preventing disease.

access.note: Anyone can read the full paper free online, so every reader can check the trial for themselves.

source.note: It appeared in a peer-reviewed exercise science journal run by a professional society, whose reviewers check each trial against its preregistered plan.

theory.note: It fills a clear gap: population studies only link long sitting to diabetes and heart disease, so this trial tests directly whether short walks change blood markers.

methods.note: Because each of 40 workers tried both days in random order, everyone acts as their own comparison; the plan was preregistered and all data are free online.

conclusion.note: It reports smaller rises in blood sugar and insulin and no change in blood fats, stresses it was a short lab test and never says the breaks prevent disease.

title: Miracle detox tea flushes out toxins and melts belly fat in 7 days
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can watch the social media video and tap its link to buy.
overview: The video says the tea 'flushes toxins' and burns belly fat. It leaves out that the liver and kidneys already clear waste from the blood. Fat also cannot be lost from one chosen spot.
methods: No study was done: the influencer only describes how she felt and measured nothing. The small print says the people in the before-and-after photos are paid models. Data availability: None.
conclusion: The influencer says the tea clears toxins and melts belly fat. The label lists senna, a laxative (a medicine that empties the bowels), which removes water, not fat. The video never mentions dehydration.
source: A fitness influencer with no science training posted the video. The tea company pays her for each sale, but the post is not labelled as an advert.

feedback.summary: There is no study, just an unlabelled advert by an influencer paid on each sale, with paid models in its photos. The claims ignore that the liver and kidneys already clear waste, while the tea's laxative removes water, not fat. Easy access is its only strength and cannot lift it off the bottom.

title.note: 'Miracle', 'flushes out toxins' and 'melts belly fat in 7 days' are advertising hype promising results that nobody measured.

access.note: Anyone can watch the video free and tap its link to buy, but easy access says nothing about whether the claims are true.

source.note: The video comes from a fitness influencer with no science training who is paid for each sale, yet the post is not labelled as an advert.

theory.note: It ignores basic biology: the liver and kidneys already clear waste from the blood and fat cannot be lost from one chosen spot such as the belly.

methods.note: No study was done: the influencer only described how she felt, measured and compared nothing and shared no data, while the before-and-after photos show paid models.

conclusion.note: The influencer claims toxin and fat loss with nothing measured, but senna, the laxative on the label, removes water rather than fat and the video never mentions dehydration.

title: Participatory budgeting linked to more civic engagement in poorer areas, compared with matched cities
access: Free to everyone online: anyone can read the paper.
overview: Participatory budgeting lets residents vote on spending part of a city's budget. It draws on ideas of deliberative democracy (citizens deciding together). This study asks whether it raises civic engagement (taking part in public life) in poorer areas.
methods: Cities chose whether to join, so the team compared N=60 cities: 30 that joined and 30 matched on income, age and ethnic mix. A preregistered analysis used voting records, plus interviews with 120 residents. Data availability: Voting data are free online; interview transcripts are on request.
conclusion: Voting and meeting attendance rose most among low-income residents. The authors say effects depended on how each city ran the scheme. They add that matched cities may still differ in ways they could not measure.
source: Published in a peer-reviewed political science journal whose reviewers check both the statistics and the interview methods.

feedback.summary: This study does well on every criterion and sits at the top of the scale. It is free to read in a journal whose reviewers check statistics and interviews. Building on democratic theory, it compares 30 cities that joined with 30 matched ones in a preregistered analysis. Voting data are open and the authors admit matched cities may still differ.

title.note: It names the policy, the matched comparison and the result in poorer areas, saying 'linked' rather than claiming the scheme caused the rise.

access.note: The full paper is free for anyone to read online, so every reader can check the methods and results.

source.note: It appeared in a peer-reviewed political science journal whose reviewers check both the statistics and the interview methods.

theory.note: It builds on theories of deliberative democracy (citizens deciding together) to ask a clear new question: whether the scheme raises civic engagement in poorer areas.

methods.note: Because cities chose whether to join, the team matched 30 joining cities with 30 similar ones, preregistered the analysis, made the voting data free online and added 120 interviews.

conclusion.note: It reports the largest rises among low-income residents, says effects depended on how each city ran the scheme and admits matched cities may differ in ways not measured.

title: Magnetic bracelets ease arthritis pain, new report finds
access: Free to everyone online: the report is a PDF on the company's shop website.
overview: The report says magnets ease pain by 'realigning the body's energy fields', but biology has found no such fields. Hospital scanners show that magnetic fields pass through the body. A small magnet's field, though, fades within centimetres.
methods: Instead of a study, the report prints letters from 18 customers who said a bracelet eased their pain. Nobody compared them with people wearing fake magnets (a placebo), though expectations easily affect pain. Data availability: None.
conclusion: The company concludes that its bracelets relieve arthritis pain and advises wearing one every day. The report does not mention systematic reviews of controlled trials, which found magnets worked no better than fake ones.
source: The company that wrote it sells magnetic bracelets for £150 each. Its website also says the magnets treat diabetes and cancer.

feedback.summary: Instead of a study, a company selling £150 bracelets prints 18 customer letters with no fake-magnet comparison. It relies on 'energy fields' that biology has not found and leaves out reviews of controlled trials finding magnets no better than fakes. A free PDF and a title without hype words cannot make up for this, so it sits at the bottom.

title.note: It avoids hype words like 'cure', but 'new report finds' makes 18 customer letters with no placebo comparison sound like a research finding.

access.note: The PDF is free for anyone to read on the company's shop website, though easy access says nothing about whether a claim is true.

source.note: The seller wrote it: the company sells the bracelets for £150 each and its website also claims magnets treat diabetes and cancer.

theory.note: It rests on 'realigning the body's energy fields', yet biology has found no such fields and a small magnet's field fades within centimetres.

methods.note: There are only 18 customer letters and no data, with no comparison against fake magnets (a placebo), which matters because expectations easily affect pain.

conclusion.note: It claims the bracelets relieve arthritis pain on the strength of customer letters alone and leaves out systematic reviews that found magnets worked no better than fakes.
